title: IS BEING SEXUALLY ATTRACTED TO SOMEONE THE SAME THING AS LUSTING AFTER THEM?
paragraphs: IS BEING SEXUALLY ATTRACTED TO SOMEONE THE SAME THING AS LUSTING AFTER THEM?
What if the thought you have been condemning yourself for is not actually the sin Jesus condemned—but what you choose to do with that thought could lead you straight into it?
There is a moment almost nobody talks about honestly.
You see someone.
Something registers.
They are beautiful.
Handsome.
Attractive.
Your body notices before you have finished forming a theological explanation for what just happened.
And suddenly, especially if you are a Christian who genuinely wants to be pure, another voice enters the room.
I sinned.
I lusted.
God must be disappointed in me.
Maybe you immediately looked away.
Maybe nothing sexual was imagined.
Maybe you did not entertain a fantasy.
Maybe you simply recognized that another human being was sexually attractive—and then spent the next hour feeling filthy for noticing.
So we need to ask the question Christians sometimes answer far too quickly:
Is sexual attraction itself the same thing as lust?
Because if we get this wrong, we can make people feel guilty for experiencing something Scripture never identifies as sin.
But if we swing too far in the opposite direction, we can rename lust “attraction,” protect our fantasies with Christian vocabulary, and excuse the very thing Jesus warned us about.
Jesus leaves room for neither shame-driven legalism nor convenient compromise.
He goes somewhere much deeper.
Into the heart.
Matthew 5:27–28 records:
Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις. ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Those words are devastating.
But notice carefully what Jesus actually says.
The Greek phrase at the center of the passage is:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pros to epithymēsai autēn.
The construction carries the idea of looking with a view toward desiring her, or looking in order to desire her.
And the verb is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō.

It can mean to desire, long for, covet, or set one’s desire upon something. The word itself is not automatically sexual or sinful in every New Testament occurrence; its moral character depends upon its object and context.
That matters enormously.
Jesus is not teaching that merely possessing eyes capable of recognizing beauty is adultery.
He is confronting something deeper.
The gaze that becomes intentional desire.
The look that doesn't merely notice but begins to consume.
The imagination that takes another person somewhere they never consented to go.
The heart that turns a human being created in God's image into material for private sexual gratification.
There is a difference between recognition and cultivation.
Between noticing and feeding.
Between temptation arriving at your door and inviting it inside.
You may not control every initial awareness that flashes through your mind.
But what happens next matters.
A person walks past you.
“They're attractive.”
That recognition can happen almost instantly.
Then comes the crossroads.
Will you honor them as a person?
Or will you mentally undress them?
Will you release the thought?
Or replay it?
Will you recognize beauty?
Or begin constructing a fantasy?
Will you see a human being with a soul...
or convert that human being into something to consume?
That is where this gets painfully personal.
Because some of us have become very skilled at changing the vocabulary without changing the heart.
“I was only looking.”
But you kept looking.
“I just think she's beautiful.”
But you deliberately revisit her pictures because of what happens inside your imagination.
“I just think he's attractive.”
But the fantasy has already become a secret room you keep returning to.
Nobody else sees it.
No messages were sent.
No physical affair happened.
No one touched anyone.
Your spouse may never know.
Your church may never know.
Your browser history might even look clean.
But Jesus walks past the locked door of outward appearances and puts His finger on the heart.
ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν... ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
Already committed adultery...
in his heart.
That is why Christ's teaching is so uncomfortable.
He does not merely ask:
“What did your body do?”
He asks:
“What did your heart want to do?”
And suddenly respectable people need grace too.
Suddenly the person who never physically cheated cannot boast.
Suddenly purity is bigger than virginity.
Faithfulness is bigger than avoiding an affair.
Holiness is bigger than maintaining a clean public reputation.
Jesus is exposing the inner world.
And perhaps that scares you because your inner world has not always been beautiful.
Maybe nobody knows what you have imagined.
Maybe you love Jesus—and still fight sexual thoughts.
Maybe you are married and sometimes notice someone other than your spouse is attractive, and the realization terrifies you.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from wondering whether every experience of sexual attraction means you have disappointed God.
Maybe pornography trained your mind for years to turn bodies into commodities, and even after repentance you sometimes feel the old pathways trying to wake up.
Maybe you have prayed...
cried...
deleted things...
installed filters...
confessed...
promised God you would never struggle again...
and then struggled again.
Hear this carefully.
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
Jesus Himself “has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet he did not sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
The existence of temptation therefore cannot itself equal sin, because Christ was truly tempted and remained completely without sin.
And recognizing that someone is attractive does not automatically mean you have committed the heart-adultery Jesus describes in Matthew 5.
But neither should that truth become permission to play games with desire.
There is a moment when noticing becomes nurturing.
When awareness becomes intention.
When attraction becomes possession in the imagination.
When you stop resisting the thought and start feeding it.
You know that moment.
It is the second look you wanted because the first was not enough.
The profile you searched for again.
The image you allowed yourself to enlarge.
The fantasy you deliberately rewound.
The conversation you kept emotionally charging because you liked how it made you feel.
The person you began imagining belonging to you sexually even though they did not.
Sometimes lust never touches skin.
It survives perfectly well inside imagination.
And Jesus loves us too much to pretend that what happens there does not matter.
But here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not expose the heart because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposes what is hidden because He came to save sinners all the way down.
Not merely our public behavior.
Our hearts.
This is the same Jesus who would go to the cross.
The same Jesus who knew exactly how corrupted human desire could become.
The same Jesus who knew every secret thought humanity would ever hide—and still stretched out His hands.
The Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself enough sexually, and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel is that sinners who could never cleanse themselves are called to repent and come to Christ, and in Him there is forgiveness, cleansing, reconciliation, and new life.
You do not defeat lust by pretending attraction does not exist.
You learn to bring your desires under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
You begin seeing people differently.
That woman is not a body placed in your path for consumption.
She bears the image of God.
That man is not a character for your private fantasy.
He bears the image of God.
That person on your screen has a history.
A family.
Pain.
Fears.
A soul.
An eternity.
And once you begin seeing people as Christ calls you to see them, lust starts losing one of its favorite weapons:
dehumanization.
Lust says, “What can I take from this person in my imagination?”
Love asks, “How can I honor this person before God?”
Lust reduces.
Love recognizes.
Lust consumes.
Love protects dignity.
Lust wants the body without responsibility for the soul.
Christ teaches us to see the whole person.
That does not mean attraction magically disappears.
Christian holiness is not becoming incapable of recognizing physical beauty.
It is learning what to do with desire when beauty awakens it.
You can notice beauty and refuse to worship it.
You can experience attraction and refuse to cultivate forbidden fantasy.
You can be tempted and run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
And sometimes the most holy prayer you can pray in that instant is remarkably simple:
“Jesus, that person is beautiful. They belong to You, not to my imagination. Teach me to see them with honor.”
Then move on.
No theatrical shame.
No self-hatred.
No pretending you didn't notice.
Just surrender.
Because shame often says, “Hide from God until you become clean.”
Grace says, “Run to Christ because you cannot make yourself clean.”
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that distinction tonight.
You have spent years believing every involuntary moment of attraction meant you were spiritually disgusting.
So every temptation became a courtroom.
Every attractive face became evidence against you.
Every bodily response became another reason to wonder whether God had finally become tired of you.
But conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Biblical conviction brings darkness into the light and calls us toward repentance and Christ.
Condemnation whispers that hiding is safer.
It isn't.
Jesus already knows.
He knew before you confessed it.
He knew before you clicked it.
He knew before you fantasized about it.
He knew before you failed again.
And the astonishing scandal of grace is not that Jesus discovered your darkness and reluctantly decided to tolerate you.
It is that the Son of God came knowing exactly what kind of sinners He was coming to rescue.
That does not make sin small.
It makes the cross enormous.
Grace is not permission to lust.
Grace teaches us that when we have lusted, failure does not have to become our permanent identity.
Repentance is still possible.
Forgiveness is still real.
Transformation is still possible.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you crossed the line long ago.
Maybe this article stopped being theoretical several paragraphs back.
Maybe you know exactly what account you need to unfollow.
Exactly which conversation needs boundaries.
Exactly which secret folder needs to disappear.
Exactly which relationship needs honesty.
Exactly what you keep calling “harmless attraction” even though you know you have been deliberately feeding it.
Then don't waste conviction.
Bring it into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Where appropriate, seek trustworthy Christian accountability.
Remove the provision you keep making for temptation.
And when you stumble, do not turn repentance into self-punishment as though your misery could add something to the blood of Christ.
Come back to Jesus.
Again.
And again.
Not casually.
Not presumptuously.
But desperately believing that the Savior who commands holiness is also the Savior who gives mercy to repentant sinners.
Some battles are won dramatically.
Others are won quietly...
one surrendered glance at a time.
One closed tab.
One honest confession.
One deleted message.
One prayer whispered while nobody else knows there is a war happening.
One decision to remember:
That person is not mine to consume.
And perhaps that is the question beneath the question.
Not simply:
“Am I attracted?”
But:
“What am I doing with my attraction?”
Am I surrendering it?
Feeding it?
Protecting it?
Fantasizing?
Coveting?
Or allowing Jesus to teach my eyes, imagination, body, and heart how to love people without consuming them?
That is a much harder question.
But it can also become a doorway to freedom.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't have to give details publicly.
But you don't have to pretend either.
And if Christ has already been healing your mind, restoring your marriage, freeing you from pornography, or teaching you how to see people differently, tell someone what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Don't excuse lust.
And don't mistake temptation for abandonment by God.
Not because giving money makes anyone more saved.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces biblical generosity through your local church or other faithful Christian giving.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from a willing heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Come to Jesus.
Not after you conquer every sexual temptation.
Not after your thoughts become spotless.
Not after you prove yourself worthy.
Come honestly.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Bring Him the attraction.
Bring Him the temptation.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the pornography history.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the secret nobody else knows.
Bring Him the part of your heart you wish you could erase.
Because Christianity is not the story of spotless people climbing high enough to reach a holy God.
It is the story of a holy Savior coming down to rescue sinners.
And maybe tonight the greatest victory will not be that you never felt temptation.
Maybe it will be that when temptation came...
you chose Jesus.
When shame said hide...
you chose Jesus.
When lust said consume...
you chose Jesus.
When failure said stay down...
you chose Jesus.
And when the enemy tried to make your worst chapter the title of your entire life...
Jesus picked up the pen.

Your temptation does not have to become your master, your failure does not have to become your identity, and your hidden chapter does not have to become your ending—because the hands holding the pen still bear the scars.
